description: I’m a Computer and Data Science student passionate about AI/ML and building practical, innovative projects. I’m looking for a motivated team with complementary skills to collaborate with, tackle the challenge creatively, and aim for an outstanding result together.
summary:
Flame in Freefall is an interactive website that turns NASA’s research on fire in microgravity into useful fire-safety information for astronauts going to the Moon and Mars.

We built a knowledge base from NASA’s ACME experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2, CFI, CFI-G and Flame Design). It contains about 2,150 pieces of information taken from final reports, requirement documents and experiment tables. Each piece shows its source, how strong the evidence is, and its limits. On the website, users can use the “Ask the Crew” chat to ask questions to a team of guide characters. The answers come from NASA records, not from guesses. The site also has charts, a smoke and flame simulation, and a space-themed journey with two visual styles: Cinematic and Retro.

NASA has produced a huge amount of data over many years, and it is spread across PDFs, spreadsheets and datasets. This makes it hard to search and compare. Our project makes the data easy to find and easy to understand, even for people who are not scientists.

This is important because flames behave differently in microgravity. Understanding them helps engineers design safer spacecraft and helps crews make better decisions.
details:
What it does and how it works

Flame in Freefall is a website that helps people explore NASA’s microgravity combustion research. We collected documents and data from the FLEX, FLEX-2, CFI, CFI-G and Flame Design investigations: final reports, requirement documents, metadata and experiment tables. A Python script converted them into about 2,150 small text chunks. Each chunk has an ID, a source, an evidence level (for example “source grounded” or “reasoned, not measured”) and a note about its limits.

When a user asks a question in the “Ask the Crew” chat, the website searches the knowledge base and selects the most relevant chunks. It sends them to a language model through an API, using a small Python server. The model must answer only from those chunks, in two to four short sentences of plain language. If the chunks do not contain the answer, it says “That is not in our data.” The server also removes sentences that mention file names, table details or other technical data-handling words, so users get science, not files. If the AI service is not available, the page shows an offline answer from the knowledge base, so the chat keeps working.

The connection to the AI is flexible. Our server works with any OpenAI-compatible API, so we can change the provider or the model without changing the website. We can use a cloud model for the best answer quality, or a local model that needs no internet connection and no API key. Because the connection is an API, the same NASA-grounded knowledge base can also be linked to other chatbots and tools in the future, such as a mobile app, a classroom assistant or a mission-planning tool.

The site also includes charts, a smoke and flame simulation, and a guided journey through the research.

Benefits

  • Scattered PDFs, spreadsheets and datasets become one place where users can search and ask questions.
  • Non-scientists can understand the results, because the AI explains them in simple language.
  • Answers are limited to NASA-based information, so the AI does not invent facts or numbers.
  • The site is honest about uncertainty and separates measured results from interpretations.
  • It is flexible: we can switch to a better or cheaper AI model when one becomes available.
  • It is reusable: other apps can use the same answers through the API.
  • It is safe: the API key stays on the server, not in the web page.

Intended impact

We want to support fire-safety thinking for future Moon and Mars missions. Flames spread, form soot and go out differently in microgravity, so easy access to the evidence can help students, engineers and mission planners learn faster and make better decisions.

Tools and technologies

  • Claude Code (Anthropic’s AI coding tool), used to build the website, the data pipeline and the server together with our team
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the website
  • Chart.js for charts, and HTML canvas for the stars, planets and flame/smoke simulation
  • Python for processing the data and exporting the knowledge base (JSON and JSONL)
  • A language model connected through an OpenAI-compatible API, with a Python proxy server that keeps the API key off the web page
  • Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which means the AI receives NASA text before it answers
  • Python with Pillow and NumPy to generate the pixel-art characters
  • Browser localStorage to remember the visual mode

Creativity

Instead of a normal dashboard, we made a space journey with a crew of pixel-art astronauts who answer questions. They are based on our own team members, and their helmets hide their faces for privacy. We also added Bondoq, our team’s cat, as an animated pixel-art character who walks around the page. Users can switch between Cinematic and Retro modes, and the science stays the same in both. This makes serious research more friendly and exciting.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: the AI can only use the retrieved NASA text, and we did not invent numbers. Weak or unverified data is clearly marked.
  • Limits of the data: PDF extraction can miss information in figures and complex tables. Results from one investigation should not be applied to another.
  • Reliability and security: the offline fallback keeps the chat working, and the API key stays on the server.
  • Cost, availability and privacy: the flexible API connection and the local-model option let us choose the best setup for each situation.
  • Accessibility and clarity: a skip link, keyboard-friendly controls and simple language.
